title: Minimizing exposure in systems handling personal information

opening.headline: When summarizing a query containing the customer's name, contact information, and account details using an LLM, which configuration minimizes exposure?
body: Using LLMs in a system that handles personal data increases the number of points where data passes through. Inputs coming to our servers, data stored by providers, information flowing back in responses, and our own logs—all become exposure points. It's difficult to say that exposing just one point reduces overall exposure.

In this course, we first learn how to mark data flow preservation points to make exposure visible. Then, we verify how de-identification, non-preservation, and log masking each reduce exposure, and we establish criteria for selecting a minimal exposure configuration by combining these three approaches in a consultation service scenario.
opening.objectivesLead: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to:
objectives: Personal data flow and storage locations can be distinguished.
The configuration with the smallest exposure range can be selected.

screens.title: In a system handling personal information, which configuration exposes the least amount of data?
screens.lead: This scenario involves a consultation service summarizing customer inquiries using an LLM. Consider the three candidate configurations and think about where exposure might occur.

visual.alt: A diagram comparing three aspects of consultation service data flow and candidate configuration.

paragraphs: The consultation service summarizes inquiries containing mixed customer information such as name, contact details, and account information using an LLM. This service consists of three main configurations: sending the entire original text verbatim, sending only the necessary portions, or sending the text with sensitive values modified.

Exposure occurs in three places. First, the volume of data being sent. Second, the data storage on the provider's side. Third, our side's logs. Each component is positioned differently between convenience and exposure. Sending the original data directly is convenient, but it increases exposure across all three locations.
This course's question is: which combination minimizes the exposure scope? The answer is not a single technique, but a configuration involving multiple layers stacked together.

callout.label: Note
callout.text: Minimum exposure does not mean giving up functionality. It means designing a system that provides the same summarization functionality while reducing the points where personal data is retained.

screens.outro: First, let's recall how well we understand the points where personal information passes through.

screens.title: Recall every point where personal data passes through
screens.lead: When you select a question, the instructor's thought process is displayed. Please try answering it yourself before clicking.

items.prompt: After the input field, how many servers and services does personal information pass through?
items.answer: Between the input interface and the API, there are often web servers, queues, pre-processing services, and provider APIs. Temporary storage may occur at each stage, and when you count the points, you find there are more than expected.

items.prompt: Does our logging and monitoring tool contain personal information?
items.answer: It is common to log the request body for debugging purposes. This log is a separate retention location, independent of the provider's no-retention option. If the original request is logged on our side, exposure remains unchanged even if the provider reduces their retention.

items.prompt: Have you distinguished between fields that must be sent and fields that can be omitted?
items.answer: Summary may require inquiry content, but account numbers might not be necessary. Sending only the required fields is the simplest and most certain way to reduce exposure. If fields are not distinguished, they typically send the entire document.

screens.outro: Now, let's indicate preservation points on the data flow to make exposure visibly apparent.

screens.title: Conservation point on data flow
screens.lead: When you select the diagram number marker, you can see which conservation occurs at each point in the flow and how it can be reduced.

visual.alt: The flowchart shown above indicates five preservation points numbered in the sequence of input, preprocessing, LLM API, response, and storage/logging.

markers.label: input
markers.title: The entire original text is sent to our server.
markers.body: The customer's inquiry contains mixed information such as name, contact details, and account information. Selecting only the required fields represents the first reduction step. At this point, the original text already exists in our server's memory and queue.

markers.label: Preprocessing
markers.title: De-identify before sending
markers.body: This is a step that detects and replaces sensitive values before being sent to an LLM. Sensitive Data Protection is documented to detect and redact PII or credential tokens in LLM prompt inputs prior to storage. This step reduces the volume of data being sent.

markers.label: LLM API
markers.title: Provider-side retention is established.
markers.body: Retention on the provider's side begins at this point. You must verify whether retention is enabled and check the abuse monitoring logs. OpenAI retains abuse monitoring logs for a default maximum of 30 days. Approved customers may implement retention exemptions or other retention controls. Gemini API logs are retained by default for a maximum of 55 days and can be set to 7, 14, 28, or 55 days. If shared as a dataset, the data may be used for training, and documentation includes a warning not to include sensitive information.

markers.label: response
markers.title: Personal information may be returned in the results.
markers.body: Personal data from the input may be directly included in the summary result. If a de-identified value was sent, the response will also contain the same token, so it is necessary to define where the original value can be restored.

markers.label: Storage · Log
markers.title: Our logs will be stored at a separate retention site.
markers.body: At the moment when results are stored or requests are logged, we establish a preservation point on our side. Since this is independent of the provider's preservation capabilities, the system must be specifically designed to only retain masked values or tokens instead of the original data.

screens.outro: Since we've verified the preservation point, let's now examine obfuscation, a prominent method for reducing the volume sent.

screens.title: De-identification methods
screens.lead: The following table lists representative de-identification methods introduced in the Sensitive Data Protection document. Compare how each method alters values and whether they can be reversed.

data.caption: De-identification Methods and Examples
rows: Erases all or part of the detected sensitive values.
Example: When the phone number is removed from "Honggil-dong Customer (010-1234-5678)", it becomes "Honggil-dong Customer".
Replace the detected value with the specified alternative value.
Replace some characters in the value with characters such as `#` or `*`.
Replace with a token encrypted with AES.
Example: "Hong Gil-dong" becomes a token such as `tok_8f3a`.
It can be rolled back depending on the method. Hash method cannot be rolled back.
35 years old becomes in the range of 30 to 39 years old.
Randomly shifts the date or retains only part of the date and time.
Example scenario: `2024-03-05` may be moved like `2024-03-17`, or only certain parts such as months may remain.
No. If in the same context, the items are shifted by the same amount, the order and duration are preserved.
data.notes: The amount and extent of information available for analysis varies by method. Deletion and masking result in minimal exposure and little residual information since the original values cannot be restored. Tokenization based on encryption converts the same value into the same token using the same key and context, preserving analytical utility while allowing restoration only when necessary. The appropriate method depends on the type of data and its intended purpose.

screens.outro: After de-identification, we will proceed with non-storage on the provider's side and log masking on our side.

screens.title: No preservation and log masking
screens.lead: Expand each item to verify the targets and limitations of the four methods.

items.title: Anonymization reduces the volume sent.
items.body: Since sensitive values are changed and sent, the original values do not reach the provider. The limitation is detection failure. Values that are not detected are transmitted as-is, and indirect identifiers that allow someone to be identified without a name may remain.

items.title: Non-preservation reduces provider storage.
items.body: An option provided by the provider that prevents storing customer content in monitoring logs such as abuse monitoring logs. OpenAI offers this to approved customers. The limitation applies to eligible features and conditions. If you use features that store state, such as file or vector storage, you must follow the retention policy of that feature, and some layers may remain depending on the provider and contract type.

items.title: Log masking reduces our exposure.
items.body: We record masked values or tokens instead of the original text in our logs. This provides a separate mechanism to reduce the number of preservation points independent of the provider's options. The limitation is that debugging becomes more difficult, so we must pre-determine which fields to include in the logs.

items.title: Reversible tokenization balances utility and exposure.
items.body: An encrypted token can only be decrypted back to its original form when absolutely necessary. We can show the model only the token, receive its response, and then restore the original data on our side—thus maintaining analytical utility while minimizing exposure. The limitation lies in key management: if the key is compromised or lost, the token becomes meaningless. Therefore, the restoration key must be stored solely on our side and never provided to the provider, and access to restoration should be strictly limited to only those individuals and systems that absolutely require it. These four methods do not replace one another but instead operate at different layers; thus, they must be co-designed together.

screens.outro: Since we have confirmed that the methods reduce different layers, I will now explain an example of combining them.

screens.title: Case Explanation: Combination of Anonymization and Non-Retention in Counseling Services
screens.lead: This is an instructor's explanation combining four methods in counseling services. Select an arrow to follow step by step and observe how the remaining data decreases at each stage.

steps.title: Detects sensitive values
steps.body: First detects names, contact information, and account numbers from the input text. Even with detection tools, some entries may be missed, so fields are excluded entirely at this stage if they are not properly identified.

steps.title: Change differently depending on the value
steps.body: Names are converted to reversible tokens so they can be restored when needed. Contacts are masked, and dates of birth are replaced with ranges. Values that do not need to be restored based on purpose are designated as non-restorable.

steps.title: Only anonymized text is sent via the lossless API.
steps.body: Only the modified text is sent via an API with the no-store option applied. This means the original values do not reach the provider, and even if some values remain, they are obscured. The functionality to save state is not used.

steps.title: We recover the response tokens only on our side.
steps.body: We revert the tokens included in the summary result to their original values only on our server. The keys are not provided to the provider. Values that do not require restoration remain masked throughout.

steps.title: Our logs contain only masked values.
steps.body: The logs contain only masked values, and we do not use features such as attaching files for state preservation. As a result, the points where personal information remains are reduced to our server's processing stage and the recovery key repository.

screens.outro: Since we've confirmed how the configuration is reduced, I'll now summarize the criteria for selecting the minimum exposure configuration using comparison.

screens.title: The criterion for selecting the configuration with the smallest exposure scope
screens.lead: Move the slider to sequentially select configurations A, B, and C. You can verify how the amount of information sent, data storage by the provider, and exposure in our logs differ across configurations.

stops.value: Configuration A: Original Transmission + Basic Preservation
stops.body: Implementation is the simplest but retains the original text in all layers. The amount of transmitted information is the highest, basic retention is applied on the provider side, and the original text may also remain in our logs. All three exposure points are large, and there are few ways to roll back.

Only anonymized values remain on the provider's side. While the amount of transmitted information is significantly reduced, the provider's baseline retention and our logs remain unchanged. If there is a detection failure in anonymization, the original data may remain on the provider's side, and the original data may still appear in our logs.

stops.value: Configuration C: De-identification + Non-preservation + Log masking
stops.body: It decreases across all three layers. The sent volume is anonymized, provider storage is non-preserved, and our side storage is reduced via log masking. The comparison criteria are the amount of sent information, provider storage, our logs, and the possibility of reversal. Due to the remaining risk of detection failure, it is not relied upon solely on anonymization but also includes non-preservation.

screens.outro: The conclusion is one: it is safest not to store it. Now let's summarize.

screens.title: Consolidation summary: It is safest to not store.
screens.lead: Let's go back to the first question and summarize. Look at the configuration that has the smallest exposure in a single flow.

paragraphs: Exposure occurs across three points: the amount of information sent, information stored on the provider's side, and information stored on our side. De-identification reduces the amount of information sent, non-retention reduces information stored on the provider's side, and log masking reduces information stored on our side. Since each individual measure only reduces exposure by one layer, all three measures must be combined to reduce exposure across all layers.

No single method is perfect. Detection failures can occur in obfuscation, acceptable functionality and conditions may be lacking in non-persistence, and debugging becomes inconvenient with log masking. Therefore, it is principle to avoid complete reliance on a single method and instead employ layered approaches.
The start is always the act of marking all preservation points within the data flow. Only visible points can be reduced. The safest configuration is one where nothing is sent and nothing is retained.

checks.intro: Please review the anonymization method and exposure reduction measures you just saw. The results are not recorded.
checks.q: What is an appropriate method for reducing personal data exposure, and what specific data exposure does it reduce?
options: No preservation reduces our side logs.
Anonymization reduces the amount of transmitted information.
Anonymization reduces our side logs only.
checks.explain: Anonymization reduces the volume sent, non-preservation eliminates provider storage, and log masking reduces our side storage. All three must be combined to reduce across all layers.

wrong.0: Non-preservation deals with storage on the provider's side.
wrong.2: Log masking handles log retention on our side.
wrong.3: De-identification occurs at the transmission stage.

checks.correctFeedback: Yes. Anonymization is a means of reducing information volume at the stage before being sent to the provider.
checks.incorrectFeedback: The means and the target have been mismatched. Review again where each means operates within the data flow.

checks.intro: Pair identification methods with their explanations. Scores are not stored, so feel free to try them out.
checks.q: Pair anonymization methods with their descriptions.
right: Generalizes a value as a range
There is also a method that converts tokens into encrypted keys and allows them to be restored.
Replaces some characters of the value with a quote-like character
Deletes all or some of the detected sensitive values
checks.explain: Each method differs in how it reduces exposure and in its reversibility.
checks.correctFeedback: Both pairs are correct. I accurately distinguished between clearing values, hiding values, converting ranges, and converting to tokens.
checks.incorrectFeedback: Some pairs are mismatched. Try re-connecting them based on whether the original values remain or can be reverted.

glossary.def: This system configuration creates the least amount of data transfer and storage.
This process involves removing, replacing, masking, tokenizing, or generalizing sensitive values.
This is an option that does not save the prompt and response to the provider side after responding.
This is a process of masking sensitive values in our logs.
This is a method that encrypts the key and allows restoring the original value when needed.

misconceptions.fact: Detection gaps may occur, and indirect identifiers may remain. Therefore, we combine non-preservation with log management.

misconceptions.myth: If the provider is non-persistent, our side logs are also cleared.
misconceptions.fact: Our logs are separate retention points independent of the provider's options. They must be masked separately.

misconceptions.myth: Masking and tokenization are the same process.
misconceptions.fact: Masking is a process of replacing certain characters with other characters, while tokenization is a process of encrypting a key to produce a token. There are reversible methods in tokenization.

closing.lead: Summarizes the key points of this class.
points: It is safest not to store it.
Anonymization reduces the amount sent, non-preservation eliminates provider storage, and log masking reduces our side storage.
Flow display shows exposure only if all preservation points are marked above.
It stacks multiple layers assuming the possibility of detection failure.
closing.reflectionLead: The following questions are intended for you to think about on your own and are not submitted or graded.
closing.reflection: When we identify all points where personal information flows through our system, where would be the most obvious area to reduce?
